name: Hydrogen peroxide gum rinse

lead: A hydrogen peroxide gum rinse is a diluted solution swished around the mouth to cut plaque bacteria and calm gum inflammation. The appearance payoff people want is gums that look less red and puffy, framing the teeth better.

It works as an antimicrobial and oxidising agent on oral bacteria and plaque. A review summarised on Wikipedia found dilute peroxide beat placebo for gingivitis and plaque, while concluding chlorhexidine is far more effective.

paras: People swish a diluted solution in the mouth as an add-on to brushing and flossing, much as other antiseptic rinses are used for home gingivitis care. Hydrogen peroxide also appears in many whitening products. Changes in gum redness are usually judged over days to weeks of routine use.

Even 3% solutions can injure the eye, so splashes need rinsing out right away. The FDA generally recognises peroxide as safe as an antimicrobial, not specifically for dental use. Anyone with persistent bleeding or swollen gums is usually directed to a dentist.

angle.text: Diluted peroxide is swished as a gum antiseptic: it reduces plaque bacteria, gum inflammation eases, and gums look calmer and healthier around the teeth. Some trials support a benefit for gingivitis, though chlorhexidine is reported to be more effective.

lead: A hydrogen peroxide gum rinse is a diluted solution of hydrogen peroxide swished in the mouth as an antiseptic. People use it for healthier-looking pink gums, a cleaner mouth and, some say, brighter-looking teeth, which all feed into how a smile looks. Hydrogen peroxide is also the active agent in many tooth-whitening products [1][2].

A review summarised on Wikipedia found a positive effect of dilute hydrogen peroxide over placebo for gingivitis and plaque, but concluded that chlorhexidine is far more effective [1]. Gingivitis articles list hydrogen peroxide among antiseptic rinses used for prevention and home treatment [3]. Wikipedia's mouthwash article describes peroxide as an oxidising rinse, such as a 1.5% product, often used short-term for acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis, that kills anaerobic bacteria and froths against debris [4].

Forum users describe long-term peroxide rinsing and report cleaner checkups and whiter-looking teeth, while dental authorities note that prolonged use can cause side effects such as enlarged papillae on the tongue [4][5].
infobox: Healthier gums, cleaner and brighter smile

paras: The cited review found hydrogen peroxide beneficial over placebo for plaque and gingivitis but much less effective than chlorhexidine.[1] A 2004 randomised trial supported a fluoridated hydrogen peroxide rinse for gingivitis.[3]

Peroxide whitens teeth by diffusing into the tooth and breaking down into free radicals that split pigment molecules into smaller, less pigmented pieces, so less light is absorbed [2]. Whitening gels are far more concentrated than a rinse: in-office gels typically hold 10-44% carbamide peroxide, roughly 3-16% hydrogen peroxide, and the EU limits retail products to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6% allowed under dental supervision [2]. Sensitivity is common after in-office whitening, and peroxide at 10% or higher can damage gum tissue, with poorly fitting trays a common cause of chemical burns [2].
Concentrations as low as 3% can be dangerous to the eye.[1] The FDA generally recognises hydrogen peroxide as safe as an antimicrobial agent, though this is not specific to dental use.[1]
Wikipedia's mouthwash article reports that side effects can occur with prolonged use, including hypertrophy of the lingual papillae [4].

A systematic review found hydrogen peroxide rinses better than placebo for gingivitis and plaque but less effective than chlorhexidine,[1] and a 2004 randomised trial supported a fluoridated hydrogen peroxide rinse.[3]

lore.intro: Peroxide mouthwash appears on T Nation as a long-running habit among lifters and as an alternative to prescription chlorhexidine.

claims.claim: A peroxide rinse calms inflamed gums and keeps plaque down.
Peroxide can stand in for prescription mouthwash.
